title: Meeting the teacher
hook: a private meeting where the student shows their understanding

segments.voice: Yesterday: sesshin, days of silent practice, and your line, gathering the mind. Which ordinary task did you do with nothing else in it? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

In the middle of a silent sesshin, one sound cuts through the hall: a small hand bell. A student gets up from the cushion, walks out, and waits in line outside a closed door. When it's her turn, she goes in, bows, and sits down across from the teacher. Just the two of them. Nobody else will hear what's said in that room. She may have a few minutes. She has to show what she understands, not explain it, not quote a book. Show it. Today's word is the name for that meeting: dokusan.
screen: `A HAND BELL IN THE SILENCE.` → `A LINE OUTSIDE A CLOSED DOOR.` → `JUST THE TWO OF THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Dokusan is Japanese, often rendered as going alone to the teacher. Not as a class. Not as a group. Alone. Whatever you've been sitting with, you carry it into that room yourself. Second, what happens inside. It differs by school. In Rinzai halls, the meeting often turns on a koan. The student presents a response, and the teacher may accept it, ask a question, or ring the bell to end the meeting, which means: go back and sit with it more. In Soto communities, dokusan is often a quieter conversation about practice: how the sitting is going, where the mind keeps getting stuck. Different shape, same doorway. Third, why it has to be face to face. Zen tradition describes itself as a teaching passed from one person to another, not only through books. A teacher can't see your understanding by reading your notes. They see it in how you walk in, how you answer, whether you hesitate or hide behind a clever line. Fourth, why it matters for someone who will never sit in that line. A lot of everyday talk about what we think happens at a safe distance: in text, in summary, after the fact. Dokusan asks for something rarer: your actual understanding, right now, in front of someone who's paying attention. Even being turned away is part of it. The bell rings, the student bows, and walks back to the cushion with the question still alive.
screen: `GOING ALONE TO THE TEACHER.` · `A KOAN, OR A TALK ABOUT PRACTICE.` · `SEEN, NOT READ.` · `YOUR UNDERSTANDING, RIGHT NOW.` · then, large: `FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then imagine a quiet room, and someone across from you who simply asks: how is your practice, really? Not the polished answer. Prepare one honest sentence. It might be, I keep starting and stopping. It might be, I don't know what I'm doing. It might be one small thing that's going well. Find that sentence, then let it rest, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dokusan. A private meeting between a Zen student and teacher, where the student shows their understanding, and the teacher meets it directly. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Today, have one conversation without a screen between you, and say one thing as plainly as you'd say it in that room. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: In Zen communities, students meet the teacher privately during retreats and regular sittings; in Rinzai practice the meeting often centers on the student's koan, while in Soto practice it is often a conversation about the student's sitting and life.

myth: dokusan is a group question-and-answer session
it's private: one student, one teacher, a closed door.
being sent back by the bell is a failure
it means go back and sit with it more; that's part of the meeting.
the student is asked to show understanding, not quote a book
the teacher looks for what you understand now, not what you've read.

fork.setup: you're in dokusan with your koan. you've prepared a clever answer from something you read. the teacher waits. what do you do?
options: show what you actually understand, even if it's 'I don't know.'
fork.reveal: the meeting is for your actual understanding, right now. a teacher may see through a borrowed answer, and the bell may send you back to sit.

original.note: Japanese: dokusan, rendered 'going alone' to the teacher. some Rinzai communities call it sanzen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a private chat with a mentor.
what it means: a short, formal meeting where the student shows, rather than explains, what they understand.
what a scholar hears: Rinzai and Soto use the same doorway differently, koan work in one, guidance on just sitting in the other, and some Rinzai halls call it sanzen.

sources.work: Zen communal practice, Rinzai and Soto

notes: Gloss of dokusan as 'going alone (to the teacher)' and the kanji 独参: confirm.
Bell details (hand bell calling students, teacher's bell ending the meeting) vary by community; described as common practice. Confirm.
Rinzai/Soto contrast stated with 'often'; the term sanzen for the Rinzai interview: confirm.
'Zen tradition describes itself as a teaching passed from one person to another' paraphrases the tradition's self-description (mind-to-mind transmission); no text cited.
Editor pass: cut an unsupported claim about why the meeting is short; softened the gloss to "often rendered".
